summary: Specifies requirements for NAT and NAPT devices that support Any Source and Source-Specific multicast, so multicast applications work better through them. It is a Best Current Practice document.

eli5.summary: Home routers that swap addresses often break group broadcasts. This lists the things such routers must do so group streams work.

questions: what igmp version must a nat support
subtitle: The rules a home or small-office router needs to follow so IP multicast keeps working through address translation.

tldr.problem: NAT devices behave inconsistently with IP multicast, which gives users flaky multicast applications and outright failures.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC lists 14 numbered requirements (REQ-1 to REQ-14) for a NAT that also acts as an IGMP proxy: leave multicast destinations alone, translate only the source, support IGMPv2 and ideally IGMPv3, and keep mappings alive long enough.
tldr.outcome: A NAT that follows the list lets multicast applications that know nothing about the NAT work as smoothly as unicast UDP does.

facts.label: IGMP support
facts.value: v1 MAY, v2 MUST, v3 SHOULD

today: RFC 5135 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 135) document published in February 2008. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Multicast Needs NAT Rules
sections.content:
For multicast applications to work well over a NAT, multicast UDP must work as seamlessly as unicast UDP. The RFC observes that NATs have little consistency in IP multicast operation, which leads to inconsistent user experiences and failed multicast.

The document targets Any Source Multicast and Source-Specific Multicast in devices that run IGMP proxy routing and NAT, without applying NAT to multicast group addresses. It names residential access routers and small branch routers as the expected setting. It is a companion to RFC 4787, the NAT behavioral requirements for unicast UDP.

PIM-SM and IPv6 are out of scope. IPv6 is excluded because NAT is not considered necessary there.
sections.eli5: Some routers rewrite addresses on everything that passes through, and that can break shows sent to a whole group at once. This RFC says how such routers should behave so group shows keep working.

sections.title: The IGMP Proxy NAT Device
sections.content:
Without a NAT, a single host connects to the DSL or cable modem directly. When one or more LANs are connected instead, a NAT device is added so that the whole network looks like a single host towards the modem. For multicast, the device does this by IGMP proxying as defined in RFC 4605, while also performing NAT.

The RFC defines two directions. 'Inside' interfaces face the hosts that want to send or receive multicast. 'Outside' interfaces are where the NAT sends IGMP membership messages and routes multicast traffic that comes from inside hosts.

IGMP messages are never logically forwarded by a proxy. They are sourced or received by it, so NAT has no impact on them: IGMP packets the device sends always use the IP address of the interface they leave from.

Multicast data is different. Unlike unicast, a multicast packet does not get its destination IP address or destination port changed. Its source IP address (and in some NAPT cases its source UDP port) is changed when it goes from inside to outside.
sections.eli5: The router acts like one person asking for shows on behalf of everyone in the house. It asks the cable company once, then hands each show to whoever wanted it.

sections.title: Forwarding and Translating Multicast Data
sections.content:
For traffic going to inside receivers, REQ-1 says a NAT MUST NOT modify the destination IP address or destination port. Otherwise it would also have to rewrite session announcements and signalling such as SAP, SIP and RTSP, which is not considered best practice. REQ-2 requires forwarding multicast UDP from outside to inside receivers, and REQ-3 says non-UDP multicast protocols (the examples are PGM and RSVP) SHOULD be forwarded too.

For senders on the inside, REQ-4 says the NAT MUST rewrite the source address to its outside address. A NAPT MUST also create a mapping so responses reach the right host. It MUST use Endpoint-Independent Mapping so hosts can learn the outside address. With several public addresses it SHOULD use Paired address pooling, so a source can discover its public address by a unicast mechanism such as ICE and tell receivers.

REQ-5 requires forwarding multicast UDP from inside to outside, with a configuration option to turn that off. Without the option, a multihomed network would cause duplicate multicast traffic on the public network.

Access links are often bandwidth-constrained, so some traffic must stay home. By default the NAT MUST NOT forward administratively scoped traffic (239.0.0.0/8, REQ-6) or the Local Network Control Block (224.0.0/24, REQ-7) from inside to outside.
sections.eli5: The router leaves the group's name tag alone but swaps the sender's return address for its own. It also keeps house-only messages inside the house.

sections.title: IGMP Version Support
sections.content:
The RFC sets a different level of obligation for each version of the group-membership protocol. A NAT MAY support IGMPv1 (the RFC calls it obsolete), MUST support IGMPv2 (REQ-9), and SHOULD support IGMPv3 (REQ-10).

For IGMPv1 and IGMPv2, a NAT can work by just relaying membership reports and queries. It MAY receive reports on the inside, NAT them, relay them and do the reverse for listeners, with no aggregation (REQ-11). If it does so it MUST NOT decrement the TTL of those messages, since they are already sent with TTL=1. Implementing IGMP/MLD proxying is still RECOMMENDED because aggregation is a useful optimization.

IGMPv3 is stricter. A NAT that supports it MUST implement IGMP/MLD Proxying (REQ-12) so that it aggregates membership reports and reports only the aggregate upstream. It MUST also implement Source-Specific Multicast and IGMPv3/MLDv2 for SSM (REQ-13).

The reason is that a NAT which interleaved reports from two reporters, joining and leaving the same groups, would produce a sequence that no single IGMPv3 reporter would send. If one host joins as another leaves and the NAT merely relays both upstream, the session is terminated, causing temporary black holing of multicast traffic.
sections.eli5: When many people in a house ask for and drop the same show, the router must combine their requests into one clean request. Passing them on separately could make the show stop for everybody.

sections.title: Any Source Multicast Senders and the Mapping Timer
sections.content:
Any Source Multicast (ASM) uses group addresses in the 224/8 through 231/8 and 233/8 through 239/8 ranges. Trouble arises when a host both receives an ASM stream and sends into it using RTP. RTP session members identify each other by source transport address and SSRC value. If the same SSRC shows up from a different transport address, members run RTP collision detection.

A NAT that only followed RFC 4787 would time out a UDP mapping after 2 minutes of inactivity. If RTCP receiver reports are sent less often than that, the host's source port changes and others see collisions, which complicates diagnostics and can disturb jitter buffer algorithms. The RFC gives an example of a group of approximately 300 members with a normal 50 Kbps audio RTP stream.

REQ-14 therefore says that when an inside host belongs to an ASM group and sends a UDP packet to that group, the NAT SHOULD use a UDP mapping timer of 60 minutes. The mapping SHOULD be destroyed when the host leaves the group, which the NAT learns from an IGMP message. If resources run out, the NAT MAY expire the mapping early, though this is discouraged, and it must still respect the 2 minute minimum mapping duration from RFC 4787.

Source-Specific Multicast does not need this long timer because feedback reports are unicast.
sections.eli5: If the router forgets a player too quickly, the other players think a stranger took their place. So it remembers group players for a long time, until they leave.

sections.title: The Requirements at a Glance
sections.content:
Section 5 repeats REQ-1 through REQ-14 as one list. In rough groups: REQ-1 to REQ-3 cover receiving multicast, REQ-4 to REQ-7 cover sending and what stays on the inside, REQ-8 to REQ-13 cover IGMP versions and proxying, and REQ-14 covers the mapping timer for ASM senders.

Appendix A adds application advice. An SSM sender behind a NAT must put its outside address in its session description (for example SDP), because SSM listeners need to know the channel as source address plus group. If several inside SSM sources pick the same group address, their traffic can no longer be told apart after NAT, and the RFC leaves that for future study. A source that does not want traffic to leave the home network can send with IP TTL=1. RTP stacks are encouraged to generate CNAMEs properly because many NATs share private address space such as 192.168.0.0/16.
sections.eli5: The rulebook ends with a checklist, plus tips for the people writing the programs that sit behind the router.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security sections of IGMPv3 (RFC 3376) and IGMP Proxying (RFC 4605) apply to a device that follows this document.

The RFC adds a note about RTCP. A host in an ASM session sends periodic RTCP receiver reports, which cause the NAT to create a mapping. For groups under approximately 300 members the reports come often enough to keep the mapping open. Above that they are rarer, and the 60 minute timer from Section 4.3 keeps the mapping open for the whole time the host takes part in the session.
sections.eli5: The rules reuse the safety advice from the group-membership rulebooks. They also make sure the router does not forget a player who speaks rarely.
